title: A good eye (Avot 2:11)
hook: an evil eye, the bad urge and hatred of people drive a person out of the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Eliezer said repent one day before you die, and nobody knows the day. Your line was repent today. Did you take one thing off the someday list? Day two hundred fifty-nine.

A friend posts a photo of her new house. You tap the heart. And somewhere under the heart, there's a small, sour feeling. Why her? She didn't even work that hard. You'd never say it out loud. But you felt it. Everybody has. Two days ago, Rabbi Eliezer's answer to the teacher's question was a good eye. Today, another of those five students, Rabbi Joshua, describes the opposite. And he says it doesn't just spoil your mood. It drives you out of the world.
screen: `THE HEART UNDER THE PHOTO.` → `A SMALL, SOUR FEELING.` → `RABBI JOSHUA'S WARNING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Joshua says three things drive a person out of the world: an evil eye, the bad urge, and hatred of people. Start with the evil eye, because it's not what you might think. In the Mishnah, an evil eye isn't a curse or a spell. It's a way of looking. A stingy, begrudging eye. The eye that sees someone else's good fortune and wishes, a little, that they didn't have it. A good eye is the opposite: an eye that's glad when others do well, and that gives freely. The Bible has a phrase for this. In Proverbs, in the old King James wording, "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor." The Hebrew there is tov ayin, literally good of eye. Then the bad urge, the yetzer hara, the pull toward the selfish thing. And hatred of people, of anyone at all. Now, why would these drive you out of the world? Commentators give several answers. One is simple: they make you miserable, and wear your life down. Another is that they cut you off. If every friend's good news stings, you slowly stop being able to be with people. You end up alone in a crowd. The good eye opens the world back up. When you can be glad for others, their joy becomes a little bit yours. And that closes a week of Hillel and his heirs: you haven't been there, be a mensch, harm comes back, more isn't more, a good heart, repent today, and now, a good eye.
screen: `THREE THINGS DRIVE YOU OUT.` · `THE EVIL EYE: A BEGRUDGING LOOK.` · `TOV AYIN: GOOD OF EYE.` · `ALONE IN A CROWD, OR GLAD.` · then, large: `A GOOD EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish one person well, for real. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose good news stung a little. A promotion, a trip, a new relationship. Don't pretend the sting isn't there. Just notice it. Then, slowly, picture them enjoying what they have. Their face. Their relief. Let yourself wish it for them, sincerely, with no but at the end. If it's hard, start small, and try again. The bell holds the time.
A good eye. Ayin tovah: a generous way of seeing, glad when others do well, the opposite of the begrudging eye that drives a person out of the world.
Your line: a good eye. Today, when someone else's good news stings, tell them congratulations and mean it. Day two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: In Jewish ethics, ayin tovah, a good eye, means generosity and gladness at others' good fortune, and it is often taught alongside the laws of giving.

match.prompt: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

myth: in the Mishnah, the evil eye is a magic curse
here it's a way of looking: stingy and begrudging of others' good.
Proverbs praises the one with a bountiful eye
he that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.
Rabbi Joshua names one thing that drives a person out of the world
three: an evil eye, the bad urge, and hatred of people.

fork.setup: a friend posts about her new house, and you feel a small sting. what would a good eye do?
options: scroll past. you don't owe anyone a heart.
be glad for her, and tell her so.
point out it's in a bad neighborhood.
fork.reveal: a good eye is glad when others do well. Rabbi Joshua says the begrudging eye drives a person out of the world.

original.note: Hebrew: a good eye, generosity of spirit.

trapdoor: what you thought: something to ward off with a charm.
what it means: a way of seeing others, begrudging or generous.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs 22:9 calls the generous person tov ayin, good of eye, the same image Rabbi Eliezer chose as the good way.

sources.quoted: He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:11 common, 2:16 in some editions.
Proverbs 22:9 is quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 is believed to read the same but was not verified.

The script says the Mishnah's evil eye is a way of looking, not a curse. Jewish folk tradition does also know the evil eye as a harmful gaze (and some Talmudic passages treat it that way); a Keeper may want a note acknowledging both.
Explanations of 'drive out of the world' (shortens life; isolates) are general summaries of commentators; confirm.
